rv.q: In Thomas Kail’s luminous and mesmerizing revival of Eugene O’Neill’s 1921 drama “Anna Christie,” which opened on Sunday at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn, Michelle Williams and Tom Sturridge play the tumultuous lovers.
Ms. Williams, under the astute direction of her husband, Thomas Kail (“Hamilton”), easily obliterates any vestiges of cliché that may cling to the character.
That Kail’s production captures its complex, tactile vitality — at once plush and grimy; Eugene was no minimalist — is, whatever the shortcomings, a real triumph.
Kail’s fleet maneuvers keep the production from bogging down without lessening the emotional combustion that is the source of the playwright's lasting genius.
All the very talented people involved would probably get a decent grade for this scene study in theater school, but it’s not a vessel fit for paying customers.
"Hamilton" director Thomas Kail brings this exceedingly bitter interpretation to the stage.
It all comes together well, but doesn’t quite turn into something great.

But director Thomas Kail smartly leans into the expressionism from that same era in his production of “Anna Christie,” opening today at St. Ann’s Warehouse; the results are a bracingly muscular stagecraft that helps create electrifying moments.
This celebrity-led revival of Eugene O’Neill’s rarely produced play offers impressive design work, even if the production as a whole doesn’t quite achieve the impact it aims for.
The production ultimately feels less like a fresh interrogation of “Anna Christie” than a respectful showcase for Williams—who is married to Kail—and a museum piece.
Director Thomas Kail—best known for large-scale Broadway musicals such as Hamilton and the recent Sweeney Todd—doesn’t seem to have a fully formed vision for the production.
Unfortunately, Thomas Kail’s uneven production doesn’t present the actress at her best; nor is her performance the standout.
This production contains the most baffling accents or accent choices on the New York stage, and the untethered polyphony hobbles the drama.
I sincerely hope that their next family affair takes place on a more seaworthy vessel.

The new St. Ann’s Warehouse revival of O’Neill’s 1921. Pulitzer winner “Anna Christie”—a collaboration between leading lady Michelle Williams and her husband, director Thomas Kail—is more of the latter, committing the cardinal sin of theater: it is unforgivably dull from start to finish.
Suffice it to say, Thomas Kail’s Anna Christie is a rare and moving dramatic experience at St. Ann's Warehouse, reaffirming O’Neill’s towering place in the American theatre.
Thomas Kail’s enthralling production at St. Ann’s Warehouse makes a strong case for this neglected earlier work.

This triumphant revival leans heavily into physical transformation, atmosphere, and emotional excavation, often finding its richest rewards in performance rather than in O’Neill’s sometimes blunt architecture.
The scenic design by Christine Jones and Brett J. Banakis and lighting design by Natasha Katz are nothing short of enchanting.
Anna Christie remains a curiosity — but one that deserves a warmer, more thoughtful embrace than it gets here.

An intoxicatingly atmospheric production and committed performance from Michelle Williams can’t disguise that Anna Christie‘s version of female empowerment involves forgiving everyone who wronged you.

With its main characters speaking and acting past each other, this Anna Christie doesn’t convincingly locate a strong rope-line from 1921 to now. Instead, it feels as unmoored as one of its barges, and overall a little lost in the muffling mists of that old devil sea.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this waterfront revival, with critics praising Michelle Williams' powerful performance but finding O'Neill's 1921 melodrama creaky and dated, despite atmospheric staging by Thomas Kail at St. Ann's Warehouse.

vr.q: Act 1 was a slog and Act 2 was stronger, but still kept spinning its wheels a lot, and I thought the whole thing could have been like 20 minutes shorter.
